title: Reverse-Angi: Shops Sell Their Overflow Jobs
one_liner: Missed calls and too-busy jobs get routed to a trusted peer shop that pays the originating shop a referral fee.
customer: Independent plumbing, HVAC, electrical, roofing and handyman shops with 1-15 techs in one metro, organized in trade circles that already vouch for each other.
problem: About 48% of home-services calls never reach a person (Invoca). Homeowners cite too-busy (21%) and no-response (14%) as barriers to hiring. Angi charges $15-85 per lead that is shared with many bidders, so shops distrust lead-gen. AI receptionists are crowded and merely take messages a shop cannot service.
solution: Shops forward busy, after-hours or out-of-scope calls to a number that answers in seconds, qualifies the job and offers it to the best-matched peer with capacity today. The job is transferred as an exclusive, pre-qualified lead. The originating shop earns a referral share of the invoice and the receiving shop pays a platform fee. Trust comes from peer vouching and network ratings. Cross-trade referrals (plumber to HVAC to electrician) are included.
why_now: In a labor-short market capacity is scarcer than demand: 73% of homeowners have unstarted projects. Lead-gen distrust is high and ServiceTitan is moving upmarket. Real-time voice AI now handles triage well enough to answer instantly.
revenue_model: 20% of transferred-job revenue paid by the receiving shop, split about 10% to the originating shop and 10% to the platform. No subscription, so no adoption friction.
non_obvious_insight: In a labor-short market leads are not scarce, capacity is. Every busy shop is currently throwing away leads, so turn each shop from a lead buyer into a lead seller. It inverts Angi's economics: shops earn money for the calls they cannot take.
first_30_days: Seed 25 shops in one metro through local association groups. Use a Twilio number and a human dispatcher first. Settle via ACH. Track transfers and conversions weekly.

title: Lights-Out Receiving Network for Driverless Freight
one_liner: On-demand night-shift dock crews plus remotely operable gates and dock doors so driverless trucks arriving at 3 a.m. actually get inspected and unloaded.
customer: Driverless-truck operators and their shipper and receiver customers, distribution centers with thin overnight staffing, and brokers offering autonomous lanes.
problem: Driverless trucks run around the clock, but most receivers have no dock labor, yard checks or inspectors at night. The CVSA enhanced-inspection clearance lasts 24 hours and requires a trained inspector, and hub-to-hub handoffs leave 'hundreds of dollars' of human cost per transfer. The PrePass/Kodiak bypass integration is live only in Texas and Louisiana.
solution: Three pieces. First, a network of trained ex-driver and yard-tech turnaround crews for walk-arounds, sensor cleaning and trailer checks. Second, a $3-6k remote gate and dock-door kit so the AV can check in and get a door. Third, on-call unload crews, with everything dispatched from one app and priced per turn below the cost of a human transfer.
why_now: Aurora is exiting 2026 with about 200 driverless trucks and targets 30,000 by 2030, California's driverless-truck rules took effect on April 28, 2026, and the Teamsters sued on August 5. Hiring retrained drivers into new roles also buys political goodwill.
revenue_model: $150-400 per truck turn, equipment lease or subscription for gate and dock kits, and a per-lane subscription for receivers.
non_obvious_insight: Autonomy shifts the constraint from driver hours to dock hours: the truck no longer sleeps, but the receiver does. The rent moves to whoever owns the human touch at the endpoints, and hiring displaced drivers turns opposition into a labor supply.
first_30_days: Pick one corridor where driverless trucks already run (for example Fort Worth to El Paso). Sign LOIs with 2 shippers on that lane for overnight receiving, recruit 10 ex-drivers or yard techs, build a simple dispatch app and target first paid turns within 90 days.

title: Insurer-Backed Self-Certified Permits for ADUs
one_liner: Japan-style private building confirmation: AI code review plus a licensed private reviewer plus an insurer-backed compliance warranty, so an ADU or small addition gets a certified package in about 48 hours where state law allows private providers.
customer: ADU builders, residential designers and architects, and homeowners in states with private-provider or third-party review statutes (Florida first), later cities piloting insured expedited review.
problem: Honolulu residential permits average 218 days (commercial 469). Government AI tools serve reviewers, and applicant-side tools for ADU owners, small builders and rural jurisdictions are thin. Faster review even increases filings (+34%) faster than permits issued (+5%).
solution: An applicant-side pre-clearance engine reads the plan set, runs the jurisdiction's zoning, structural and energy rules, and returns a correction list in minutes. A licensed private provider signs, and a surplus-lines policy from an MGA indemnifies owner and jurisdiction against code errors, priced from the engine's error data. Where private-provider laws exist the package is submitted directly, and elsewhere it is offered as an insured fast-track pilot.
why_now: Government pilots prove review can be automated (Honolulu review cycles down 58%, Denver's $4.6M contract). LLMs can now read plan sets. The ROAD Act funds standard blueprints. Insurers are hunting for new specialty lines, and applicants are desperate.
revenue_model: $1,500-3,000 per ADU permit package. 10-15% share of warranty premium. SaaS for designers.
non_obvious_insight: Governments will never build the applicant-side tool because of conflict of interest, but insurance can do what regulators cannot: price and carry the residual risk that a bad plan slips through. Japan has let designated private bodies issue building confirmations since the late 1990s, and permit timelines there are days, not months.
first_30_days: Partner with a Florida private-provider firm. Run 20 ADU and remodel plan sets free for three designers and compare predicted corrections to actual city comments. Pre-sell to ADU builders at $1,500 and show the accuracy data to two MGAs.

title: Groundskeepers: Custodianship for AI-Built Software
one_liner: Property management for software: a monthly subscription where a named junior-developer 'groundskeeper' keeps small businesses' AI-built apps patched, backed up, monitored, and alive, with a senior signing off.
customer: SMBs (multi-location dentists, HVAC firms, property managers, boutique agencies) and solo founders who built internal tools or products with Lovable, Replit, Cursor and similar. $149-499/month per app. Agencies that built apps for clients can white-label.
problem: Building is free but owning is not. 'Vibe-code cleanup' is a recognized freelance niche, but it is a one-time project. After the rescue no one is responsible for dependency updates, key rotation, backups, uptime, model deprecations, and API changes, and a large share of production vibe-coded apps hit an incident within 90 days.
solution: A fixed-price move-in inspection ($900), then a monthly custody plan with monitoring, patching, backup verification, a lightweight quarterly security check, a runbook, and one accountable human with an incident SLA. Groundskeepers are laid-off junior developers, each managing 25-40 apps on a standardized template stack with AI tooling, supervised by fractional seniors. The plan includes an 'exit ramp' to rebuild or retire the app.
why_now: In 2026 a flood of AI-built apps entered production and cleanup specialists are one of the fastest-growing freelance niches, per Forbes coverage. Junior developer hiring has dried up, so skilled, cheap talent is abundant. Cyber insurers are beginning to care about managed versus unmanaged apps.
revenue_model: Recurring subscription, inspection fees, incident retainers, exit-ramp rebuilds, and referral fees from cyber insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The market frames this as cleanup (a project) but the durable business is custody (a relationship), like property management versus house flipping. The same structure gives displaced juniors a career ladder: custody is the residency that produces the senior engineers the industry stopped training.
first_30_days: Offer free move-in inspections to the first 20 apps through Lovable and Replit communities, local chambers of commerce, and SMB Facebook groups. Hire 2 laid-off juniors. Assemble monitoring from off-the-shelf tools (Sentry, uptime checks, Dependabot). Target 15 paying customers at about $199, roughly $3k monthly recurring revenue, by day 90.

title: Open-Banking Rails for EU Connected Products
one_liner: A consent-and-access hub that lets manufacturers meet the EU Data Act's access-by-design duty and lets owners route product data to repairers, insurers and energy optimizers through one integration.
customer: Two sides. Forced buyers are manufacturers, importers and white-labelers of connected products sold in the EU (e-bikes, heat pumps, wallboxes, appliances, machinery, agricultural kit, wearables), paying per product family per year. The network side is independent repair chains, insurers, energy retailers, lenders and fleet managers paying per authorized device pull.
problem: Since 12 Sept 2026, connected products newly placed on the EU market must give users free, structured, machine-readable access to their data and share it with third parties on request. Most SME makers and importers have cloud endpoints never designed for this: no consent flow, no standard API, no logging, no trade-secret safeguards, no pre-sale disclosures. Third parties who want the data face hundreds of separate negotiations.
solution: A hosted 'Data Act portal' for the manufacturer covering ownership binding (QR or serial on the product), machine-readable export, consent to share with a named third party, trade-secret safeguards, access logs, a dispute workflow and the Art. 3(2) pre-contract disclosure templates. A normalized schema catalog per product category (for example 'heat pump v1') means third parties integrate once. We sell it first as a 90-day compliance kit, then monetize the network.
why_now: The access-by-design duty took effect 12 Sept 2026 and law-firm alerts show many makers unfinished. From 12 Jan 2027 cloud switching fees vanish, which makes data mobility a political priority. The regulation mandates giving data but says nothing about how anyone receives it.
revenue_model: Compliance SaaS at roughly EUR 300-3,000/month per product family. Network fees of EUR 0.02-0.50 per device per month from third-party consumers of the data. An optional certification badge for makers.
non_obvious_insight: The Data Act is open banking for machines, but with no PSD2-style standardization mandate: it creates a duty to give data with no way to receive it. Whoever standardizes the receiving side becomes the Plaid of physical products. The manufacturers, who are forced buyers today, pay for the network build.
first_30_days: Pick one fragmented vertical (e-bikes, or heat pumps and wallboxes). Publish a free 'is my product in scope' checker and a readiness checklist to generate leads. Sign 5 SME makers or importers to EUR 2k pilots that deliver a working access endpoint. Pitch two independent repair, insurance or energy firms as first consumers on the receiving side.

title: Vendor-neutral body-cam redaction bureau with fee pass-through
one_liner: A CJIS-cleared remote team that returns double-reviewed redacted police video priced per minute below the fee small cities already charge requesters, so the bureau funds itself.
customer: Small police departments and sheriff's offices (roughly 5-60 sworn officers) with records backlogs, and the city clerks and attorneys who carry the liability. They pay $0.40-0.60 per video minute plus a small monthly minimum.
problem: Small agencies do not have redaction staff. Elko, NV's police chief described about a year of catching up on redaction requests with no full-time redaction team and approved a five-year Axon extension of about $91,200 a year. White Salmon, WA has only two trained employees and set a $0.84-per-minute redaction fee (4-1 vote, April 15, 2026) while the chief said he 'cannot readily add a second-review step for all releases' because of limited trained staff and high request volume. A councilor dissented, arguing that sensitive footage such as juveniles needs more than one reviewer. Phoenix has nearly 40,000 pending public-records requests and raised commercial fees to pay for staff. AI-generated request floods (Somerset County, PA saw dozens a day) make it worse.
solution: A regional redaction bureau. Departments send only the clips requested (through share links from Axon, Motorola/WatchGuard, Getac and Wolfcom or others) and get back redacted video plus a redaction log within 5 business days. Automated face, plate and audio detection does the first pass. Then two trained human reviewers sign off, with a state-specific checklist (juveniles, victims, medical, informants). The bureau also sells 'backlog amnesty sprints' at a flat rate to clear a year-old queue. Vendor neutrality is the selling point, since Axon's automated redaction only helps agencies inside its ecosystem and still requires manual verification.
why_now: Body camera adoption is nearly universal after 2025-2026 contract cycles (Elko, Plainview, Crescent City, Carlsbad, Kasson approvals), public-records volume is up, and states are formalizing per-minute cost recovery. Councils are now adopting the fee schedules that make a pass-through model possible.
revenue_model: Per-minute fee ($0.40-0.60) billed to the agency, which recovers most or all of it from requesters at its own per-minute fee (White Salmon: $0.84); monthly minimum of $250; flat-rate backlog sprints of $5k-20k.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not blurring speed, it is a defensible second review on sensitive content, which small departments cannot staff. The fee schedule councils are adopting is derived from a cost-of-service study, so the department can pass the bureau's cost straight through; the bureau's margin lies between its price and the city's published fee. CJIS clearance and background checks form the moat that keeps generic video-AI startups out. Evidence: Elko's year-long backlog (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/7804457/nevada/elko-county/elko-city/elko-approves-five-year-axon-contract-for-body-cameras-and-redaction-software-to-clear-backlog); White Salmon's two trained employees, the $0.84/minute fee and the second-review dissent (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/8492326/washington/klickitat-county/white-salmon/council-updates-public-records-policy-approves-084-per-minute-body-camera-redaction-fee-over-staff-objections); Phoenix's roughly 40,000 pending requests (https://www.kjzz.org/politics/2026-09-24/commercial-public-records-requests-prices-have-gone-up-in-phoenix-in-effort-to-hire-more-staff).
first_30_days: Pick one state, such as Washington, with strong public-records laws and many small departments. Sign the CJIS security addendum with 2 agencies and have all reviewers fingerprint-cleared. Find 15 departments with a visible backlog in recent council minutes and offer a flat 'backlog amnesty sprint' on their first 500 minutes at $0.45/min. Turn the state's checklist into a review template and deliver the first 3 jobs within the month.

title: Escaped-Burn Liability Cover Verified From Orbit
one_liner: Go/no-go data and liability cover for prescribed burn associations, priced from fuel dryness and settled by satellite proof that the fire never left the unit.
customer: Prescribed burn associations, contract burn bosses and private landowners (ranchers, forest owners) in Texas, Oklahoma, the Great Plains, the Southeast, Colorado and the West Coast. Surplus-lines MGAs, insurers and state forestry agencies are the second customer.
problem: Prescribed fire is the cheapest wildfire-adaptation tool, but escaped-fire liability cover is described as 'unavailable, unaffordable and vital' in places like Oregon and Colorado. Only a few risk pools exist, such as three Georgia burn associations with about 1,600 members. Insurers cannot price it because after an escape nobody has objective evidence of what was burned or when.
solution: Phase 1 is a software and certificate business that needs no insurance licence. A per-burn pack combines satellite live fuel-moisture and soil-dryness signals with forecasts as a documented go/no-go. A 72-hour containment certificate compares thermal hotspots (VIIRS, FireSat, commercial thermal) and next-day burn-scar perimeter (Sentinel-2 and Landsat at 10-30 m) against the permitted unit. Phase 2 has a partner MGA or risk retention group underwrite association pools, with verification making claims close to binary.
why_now: FireSat's first three operational satellites (July 2026) will deliver at least twice-daily data to early adopters by end-2026, heading to about 20 satellites and hourly revisit by 2029. Suppression backlogs and insurance retreat are pushing states to legalise more burning, and the Nov-Apr burn season starts within weeks. New free 10-30 m optical and radar archives make unit-level perimeter checks nearly free to produce.
revenue_model: $95-$250 per burn certificate plus $1.50-$3 per acre. Association memberships of $1-3K/yr. Later, MGA commission or a data licence to insurers underwriting pools.
non_obvious_insight: Prescribed fire is uninsurable not because it is risky but because nobody can prove afterwards that it stayed inside the line. An objective, cheap orbital perimeter check turns an unpriceable moral-hazard argument into an auditable event. Gross-negligence liability standards in state burn laws turn on documented preparation, which the go/no-go pack supplies.
first_30_days: Offer free winter-season pilots to 10 burn associations (TX, OK, NE, GA, CO) and build the containment check on free VIIRS, Sentinel-2 and Landsat data while applying for FireSat early-adopter access. Start charging $95 per certificate from December. Get one surplus-lines broker or MGA to review the certificate format as the seed of a Phase 2 pool.

title: Drive-By Lawsuit Shield for Marketing Stacks
one_liner: Scan and fix the text, website and review flows that trigger serial-plaintiff demand letters, and back it with a response pack.
customer: Local-service SMBs and small multi-location brands, sold mostly through local marketing agencies and agency resellers on GoHighLevel, Wix and Squarespace.
problem: Serial-plaintiff waves target small firms: text-message consent and quiet-hours claims, website accessibility claims, wiretap claims over chat widgets and tracking pixels, and the FTC's fake-and-gated-review rule (prior knowledge on the rules). Demands of $5-25k get settled blind. AI-generated marketing raises exposure: 83% of AI-using small firms use AI for writing or marketing.
solution: A scanner checks known triggers: SMS consent capture and state quiet hours, trackers and chat widgets without consent banners, basic accessibility failures, review-gating flows and unsubstantiated claims. It applies or guides fixes, keeps a provenance-stamped consent ledger, and provides a demand-letter response pack via a partner law firm. Defense-cost coverage can be added through an MGA.
why_now: SMBs are now running automated texting, AI-written content and review requests, and small businesses lack legal capacity to evaluate demands.
revenue_model: $19-49 per site or number per month, $499 per response pack, plus a share of insurance premiums.
non_obvious_insight: The vendor who sells the marketing tool never gets sued, but the owner does, and the agency is liable to its client. The buyer of protection is the agency reseller, not the owner.
first_30_days: Build scanners for three triggers and run free scans on 500 local sites. Sell reports to 10 agencies and sign a law-firm partner for the response pack.

title: Fire-Line Readiness Passport for Contract Wildfire Crews
one_liner: A qualifications, equipment-inspection and shift-ticket system for private wildland fire engine and crew owners, built so they are never rejected at check-in or paid late.
customer: Owners of private wildland fire engines, hand crews and water tenders contracted by federal and state agencies (the national association alone represents 300+ contractors). A single rig or crew can gross six figures in a season.
problem: Contract fire resources are dispatched from agency lists and must show current qualifications, red cards, fitness tests, insurance, vehicle and pump inspections and correct rate documentation. A missing or expired item gets the rig rejected or sent home at check-in. Payment then depends on shift tickets being filled out and reconciled correctly. Errors mean holds and weeks of waiting while the owner fronts payroll, fuel and insurance. Most operators run this on paper and text messages.
solution: A mobile passport per crew member and rig. It tracks qualification and training expiry, physical and medical dates, insurance certificates and equipment checklists against the specific contract's rules. It flags what will fail at check-in, generates GPS-and-time-stamped shift tickets in agency format with automated checks against contract rates, and packages payment documents. Later it adds accelerated payment.
why_now: Agencies are leaning heavily on contractors, the national Type 2-IA crew contract cycle continues through 2026-27, and the wildfire workforce and pay rules are shifting. It is late September, so the off-season sales window for 2027 contracts is open and there is time to build an MVP before next season.
revenue_model: $150-400 per engine or crew per month. A 1-2% fee on accelerated payment advances against verified, error-free packets, once the record system proves low rejection rates. Insurance and training referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: In fire contracting, the paperwork is the collateral. The rig-days lost to rejection and the payment delays from ticket errors are the real costs. A system that pre-validates packets against the contract's own rules is trusted by agencies, insurers and factoring companies alike, so it can become the data layer for everything financial in the niche. The market looks small (roughly a thousand firms), but each firm has an unusually high willingness to pay.
first_30_days: Join the national contractor association's conversations and contact owners on state preseason contract lists in Oregon, Idaho, Montana and California. Offer a $750-1,500 'pre-season readiness audit' per rig, mapping each contract's checklist. Use the audits to design the MVP. Sell subscriptions from February for the 2027 season.

title: EUDR reference-number desk for downstream buyers
one_liner: An inbox-and-validator service that collects, checks and vaults EUDR reference numbers and plot GeoJSON from suppliers, sold to downstream operators and via customs brokers.
customer: Mid-size EU importers, traders and manufacturers who buy EUDR goods (wood and furniture components, coffee, cocoa, leather, rubber parts, palm derivatives) after a first operator has placed them on the market. The second channel is customs brokers and freight forwarders who white-label the desk.
problem: From 30 Dec 2026, large and medium operators and traders must comply. Downstream operators no longer file due diligence statements but must collect and keep upstream reference and verification numbers for 5 years. They cannot place goods on the market if the numbers are missing when evidently required. One guide estimates 15-30 minutes per supplier per plot for chasing, format fixes and plausibility checks, which is 'several person-weeks' at 150 suppliers, every year. Typical data faults are self-intersecting polygons from phone apps, areas off by 100x, national coordinate systems instead of WGS 84, plots outside the declared country and duplicates.
solution: A forward-to inbox and portal that (1) extracts reference and verification numbers and GeoJSON from supplier emails, PDFs, spreadsheets and invoices; (2) runs geometry checks on closed rings, self-intersection, WGS 84 with six decimals, the 4-hectare polygon rule, plot inside the declared country, duplicates and area versus tonnage plausibility; (3) auto-sends the supplier a plain-language fix request in their language, with a mobile-friendly plot-drawing link; (4) keeps a 5-year evidence vault; and (5) shows a per-purchase-order 'safe to ship or resell' status. Ship a free public GeoJSON validator first as the lead magnet.
why_now: The 30 Dec 2026 application date is fixed. The Commission's May 2026 review said the regulation will not be reopened and proposed a wider product scope through a draft delegated act, so more mid-size buyers will be pulled in. The EU TRACES NT system was reported not fully operational for the December 2025 date, so integration surprises remain.
revenue_model: SaaS tiers of EUR 79-249 per month by supplier count, plus EUR 1-3 per consignment checked. White-label to brokers at EUR 0.50-3 per declaration or a flat EUR 500-2,000 per month. Optional paid supplier-data cleanup projects.
non_obvious_insight: Filing software is crowded, but 'no DDS needed' makes downstream buyers feel safe while they inherit the messiest job: chasing numbers by email from dozens of suppliers, with a 5-year retention duty and a day-one commercial gate. As one guide puts it, 'Market access, not the fine, is the mechanism that will change behaviour first', because customers cannot resell goods without the numbers (https://www.omnia-analytics.at/en/blog/eudr-2026-operator-data-requirements, which also gives the 15-30 minute estimate and the polygon error list). Incorrect polygon format is reported as a leading cause of DDS rejection (https://www.coolset.com/academy/eudr-geolocation-requirements-how-to-collect-and-validate-gps-polygon-data-for-your-dds). Manufacturers 'do not consider themselves agricultural commodity buyers' yet inherit the duty (https://www.regilient.ai/blog/eudr-due-diligence-product-traceability-compliance). Fixing data at the supplier gives free viral distribution, because each supplier serves many buyers.
first_30_days: Build the public GeoJSON checker using open geometry libraries and rank it for searches like 'EUDR GeoJSON self-intersection error'. Pitch 3 customs brokers and 3 coffee, timber or furniture importers with a manual concierge version: they forward supplier emails and you return a cleaned register within 48 hours. Charge EUR 500 for a one-off audit of their existing supplier files. Use the audits to find the 10 most common data faults and build fix templates.

title: Provably Anonymous, Provably Employee Whistleblower Channel
one_liner: A reporting channel where a worker proves they hold a company email using zero-knowledge proofs, without the employer or vendor ever learning who they are.
customer: EU and UK employers with 50-500 staff that must run internal reporting channels, employment-law and compliance firms that deploy them, and works councils.
problem: Whistleblower-directive compliance is often a checkbox. Employees do not believe 'anonymous' hotlines that log IPs and identities, so use is low. Employers get junk or spoofed reports and cannot confirm that a reporter is a real current employee.
solution: ZK-email proofs of an employer-domain, DKIM-signed message let a reporter prove employment without revealing which mailbox. Per-report nullifiers block duplicates, and no identity is stored. Add anonymous two-way messaging, evidence upload, and a 'verified current employee in a group of at least 10' signal to the company. Independent cryptographic review is published.
why_now: ZK-email tooling is open source and maturing, EU digital-identity wallets are due by end 2026, and deepfake and spoofed reports are increasing. Whistleblower rules now apply to smaller firms, so many companies are buying cheap channels for the first time.
revenue_model: EUR 300-1,500 per month per company, with a 30% channel margin for law firms and a free tier for firms under 50 staff.
non_obvious_insight: Hotline usage is limited by trust in anonymity, which promises cannot improve, only making identification cryptographically impossible can. The same proof gives employers what they want (verified employee) and gives hostile insiders nothing.
first_30_days: Prototype with open-source zk-email libraries. Line up three employment-law firms and 10 SMEs for a free pilot, and commission a small third-party cryptography review to publish.

title: Guest-Funded Wildfire Hardening for Vacation Rentals
one_liner: An opt-in per-night 'fire-safe stay' fee that lets guests pay down the ember-proofing of the vacation homes they rent, unlocking insurance credits and renewals for owners who cannot afford the retrofit.
customer: Owners and property managers of vacation rentals and cabins in wildfire-exposed resort towns (Lake Tahoe/Truckee, Big Bear, Mammoth, Idyllwild, Estes Park, Ruidoso, Gatlinburg, Sunriver) facing nonrenewals or multiples of prior premiums. Insurers writing in distressed ZIPs are a secondary payer for leads.
problem: Retrofit baselines run $8K-25K while insurer discounts are only 5-35%, so owners cannot front the cash and the credit is unclaimable in practice. Short-term rentals are the least tolerated use for carriers. Owners are dropped over aerial-imagery roof photos and then have to prove their case. Yet these homes throw off daily cash flow, and their occupants are unfamiliar visitors with the highest life-safety exposure.
solution: An opt-in $3-6 per night fee at checkout (direct-booking sites and partner property managers) pools into a retrofit financing note for that specific house. Vetted crews install ember-resistant vents, roof and gutter fixes and 5-foot-zone clearing to the IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home standard. We build a time-stamped evidence pack (photos, receipts, certificate) and file it with the insurer under the new mitigation-credit and dispute rules. Guests see a public 'hardened home' badge. Owner pays nothing up front, and the fee stream repays the financier over 3-5 years.
why_now: Rules now force insurers to credit and explain: Colorado HB25-1182 has applied since 1 July 2026 (score disclosure, documented-mitigation credit, appeal) and California AB 75 (notice, photo copies, remediation window) went operative 1 July 2026. IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home just expanded to Washington, signaling national scale. California launched a Safe Homes Grant and a revolving loan program. An FTC all-in-pricing rule for short-term lodging (effective May 2025) makes an opt-in structure the clean design.
revenue_model: 15-20% take of the surcharge flow, financing spread on the retrofit note, 3-5% contractor referral fee, and an insurer or MGA lead fee per credited policy or renewal.
non_obvious_insight: A vacation rental is the rare residential asset with a daily, price-insensitive cash stream that can service a retrofit loan, and guests are exactly the people the hardening protects. That aligns payer and beneficiary. Insurers hate short-term rentals most, so documented hardening changes the underwriting conversation where it matters most.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 owners through Big Bear and Truckee property managers. Get one local roofer or vent installer to give fixed-price bids. Add the opt-in fee line through an existing direct-booking tool (Hospitable, OwnerRez or Lodgify style widgets) and measure guest opt-in rate. Line up a $100-250K revenue-based note from a small local lender or angel. File the first evidence packs with two carriers.

title: Craft Data: Retiring Machinists Teach Robots
one_liner: Pay shops to let experienced craftspeople wear cameras and gloves, and sell the captured factory-floor skill data to robot-learning labs.
customer: Robot foundation-model and humanoid companies buying training data. Shops are the second customer, receiving cash and auto-generated standard work instructions.
problem: Physical AI funding hit $18.6B in Q2 2026, but labs lack high-quality real-world industrial manipulation data (setups, fixturing, deburring, measuring by feel). Meanwhile a retiring workforce takes unrecorded tacit skill, and no dataset of it exists.
solution: An egocentric capture kit (head and wrist cameras, instrumented glove, audio narration) worn during normal work. Add job context from CAM programs and travelers. Deliver curated, annotated datasets to labs. Shops receive setup videos, SOPs and a training library, and workers share in revenue, with consent, IP and safety protocols agreed up front.
why_now: Record physical-AI funding, cheap wearable capture hardware, imitation-learning advances, and a retirement wave. Labs need real industrial data, not lab data.
revenue_model: Target $150-400 per curated hour from labs (to validate with first buyers). Pay shops about $40 an hour. $500 a month per shop for the SOP and training library.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input to robot learning is expertise, not compute. The same footage is a shop's best defense against retirement knowledge loss, so shops will host the capture and even pay for the by-product.
first_30_days: Recruit five shops with free SOP videos as the hook. Capture 100 hours. Pitch five labs with samples. Aim for one paid pilot of $20-50k. Hire an employment lawyer for consent and IP terms.

title: Multi-Rail Cash-Flow Underwriting After UPI Fees
one_liner: When UPI stops being free for big tickets, reconstruct small-merchant revenue from GST, bank and supplier data instead of UPI alone.
customer: NBFCs, small finance banks and cash-flow lenders that lend to kirana and small retail businesses.
problem: Lenders assumed UPI data was the universal truth for underwriting. The Oct 15 MDR (0.4% above Rs 2,000, capped at Rs 300) hits about 4% of P2M volume but about 66% of value, so merchants now have a reason to route big tickets through cash or bank transfer.
solution: An API that combines Account Aggregator bank data, GST e-invoice and filing data, supplier invoices and soundbox/QR data into a revenue estimate with a rail-shift adjustment. The wedge is a turnover sanity-check score for five NBFCs.
why_now: MDR starts Oct 15, the Supreme Court refused a stay, and retailers are organising protests. RBI's cash-flow lending push depends on this data.
revenue_model: Rs 40-120 per scored application plus a monitoring fee on the live loan book.
non_obvious_insight: A fee on exactly the high-value 66% creates an incentive to hide it. The rail shift is a data-quality shock, and the first lender to model it gets an underwriting edge.
first_30_days: Get consented data on about 200 existing borrowers from one NBFC partner and backtest against repayments. Offer a 60-day free pilot.

title: Moonlighting and IP Clearance for AI Experts
one_liner: A concierge that checks and files the employer-disclosure, IP-assignment and confidentiality paperwork professionals need before moonlighting as AI-training experts, and issues clean-provenance certificates that labs and vendors can rely on.
customer: Employed lawyers, bankers, doctors, consultants and engineers doing expert-data gigs pay $79-149 per clearance. Data vendors and lab legal or procurement teams pay for an annual B2B license.
problem: Millions of experts have signed up, many still employed at banks, law firms and hospitals with outside-activity approval rules (e.g. FINRA-registered staff), IP assignment and confidentiality duties. Some platforms even solicit prior work that former employers may own (HN Apr 2026). One trade-secret suit could freeze a vendor's programs, and workers risk termination or licence discipline.
solution: (1) A contract reader flags moonlighting, IP and confidentiality risk in the worker's agreement and handbook. (2) Templates for the employer disclosure or approval request. (3) A scanner for confidential markers in submitted work. (4) A 'clean-room certificate' per contributor. (5) An onboarding API vendors can require. A partner attorney covers the advice.
why_now: The Mercor breach and class actions have made vendor risk teams and lab counsel nervous. Reports of labs asking contractors for real past work samples raise provenance stakes. The scale of professionals moonlighting for AI companies is unprecedented.
revenue_model: Per-clearance fee for workers plus $50-250k annual vendor licences and per-contributor API fees.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer with money is the vendor's general counsel, not the worker, but the worker channel gives distribution and data. A database of moonlighting and IP policies for the top few thousand employers, built from worker submissions, becomes the moat.
first_30_days: Interview 20 moonlighting experts. Hand-build 50 employer-policy profiles (big banks, Big 4, large law firms, health systems). Run a manual $99 concierge clearance service. Pitch two mid-tier data vendors' compliance leads a paid pilot.

title: Year-Three Warranty Claims Agent and Failure Index
one_liner: An agent that files manufacturer, retailer and credit-card extended-warranty claims when your stuff dies, paid on success, whose claims data becomes a durability index that Amazon's star ratings cannot provide.
customer: Consumers who bought $200 to $3,000 durables (appliances, e-bikes, laptops, mattresses, power tools) in the past 1 to 4 years. Later data buyers: home-warranty and insurance firms, retailers, brand quality teams and AI shopping agents.
problem: Amazon's incentives end at the return window, and reviews freeze at week two, but failures happen in year two to four. The money left behind sits in three layers: manufacturer warranties, retailer protection plans and credit-card extended warranty. It goes unclaimed because people cannot find the receipt, do not know which layer applies, or quit at the phone tree. Meanwhile shoppers have no independent durability signal, and the one consumer tool for spotting fake reviews, Fakespot, was shut down by Mozilla in July 2025 for lack of a business model.
solution: The consumer connects a receipt source (read-only, receipts only, opt-in) and the agent builds a coverage ledger for big purchases: warranty end dates, card-benefit eligibility, retailer plan status. When the user texts that the dishwasher died, the agent assembles the claim packet (receipt, serial number, photos, symptom), files with the right layer over email, chat or a voice agent, and chases it to resolution. Every outcome (brand, model, failure mode, age at failure) goes into an anonymized Failure Index.
why_now: LLM agents can now read messy receipts and run multi-channel claims at a cost per claim low enough for a success-fee model. AI shopping assistants and agentic checkout need trustworthy durability signals, which star ratings do not supply. Fakespot's 2025 shutdown proved consumers will not pay to check reviews, so the payer has to be the claim recovery itself.
revenue_model: A success fee of 20% to 25% of recovered value (refund, repair or replacement), or $19 flat per filed claim. In year two, license the Failure Index by API or report to warranty administrators, insurers, retailers and shopping agents ($2k to $25k per month). Affiliate referrals for a better replacement at the moment of failure.
non_obvious_insight: The unowned moment in commerce is month 25, not the purchase. Every incumbent (Amazon, brands, card issuers) profits when claiming is hard, and a failure someone bothered to claim is a labeled ground-truth data point, unlike a star rating. Sell claims recovery to consumers, who will pay, and the byproduct dataset is what the institutions that price durability will pay for.
first_30_days: Run it concierge-style. Put up a landing page: 'Did your appliance, e-bike or laptop die within 3 years? We file the claim, you pay only if we recover.' Recruit 30 claimants from Reddit (r/appliances, r/ebikes) and local Facebook groups. Draft claims with an LLM and send them by hand, logging every outcome. Pick one category (for example e-bike batteries or robot vacuums) and publish five public posts on what the claims data shows. Approach one home-warranty or appliance-retail company for a paid data pilot.

title: Defensibility Desk for GenAI Document Review
one_liner: An independent validation service that samples, blind-reviews and documents the accuracy of AI-assisted document review so litigators can defend it to opposing counsel and judges.
customer: Litigation partners and e-discovery leads at mid-size firms (25-500 lawyers), corporate litigation departments, and ALSPs and e-discovery vendors moving first-pass review to LLMs.
problem: ALSPs are consolidating around AI-enabled workflows 'engineered around human review' (Repario acquired UnitedLex on 28 Sep 2026). Review has moved from TAR to LLM classification, and opposing parties and judges will ask for proof of recall and precision. Self-validation by the team that ran the review is neither independent nor consistent, and there is no accepted protocol for LLM review.
solution: A standard protocol: statistical sampling (elusion and recall estimates with confidence intervals), blind second-pass review by a bench of reviewers, adjudication of disagreements, drift checks across model versions, and a court-ready validation declaration with optional expert testimony. It plugs into Relativity, Everlaw and DISCO by API.
why_now: Generative-AI first-pass review went mainstream in 2025-26, private equity is rolling up ALSPs on the promise of AI plus human review, and judges are scrutinizing AI use in litigation.
revenue_model: $4-20k per matter validation, $60-250k/year programs for ALSPs, and hourly expert testimony.
non_obvious_insight: AI drives first-pass review cost toward zero, which makes independent validation the billable, defensible act, and independence is what gives it evidentiary weight (like an auditor). Displaced contract reviewers are a ready workforce for it.
first_30_days: Interview 15 e-discovery counsel and design the protocol with a statistician advisor. Run three pilot validations at $3-5k on closed matters and publish the protocol as a whitepaper to build credibility.

title: Teleoperated Trenching Crews for Infill Lots
one_liner: A control room of remote operators driving retrofitted compact excavators and skid steers on residential lots (utility trenching, pad grading, backfill), sold per linear foot.
customer: Small and ADU builders, factory-built home dealers needing site work, and small site-work contractors short on operators.
problem: Site work and foundations are the first constraint (foundations wait 30+ days; 15-20 houses stuck on foundations for 6+ weeks). Operators are aging out and are poached by larger jobs. Small residential jobs waste an operator's day on travel and waiting.
solution: Rental compact excavators fitted with joystick actuation, cameras, cellular or satellite bonding and a geofence kill-switch. Operators, including 55+ or injured veterans, run machines from a control room, one job after another across a metro, while a local machine tender handles spotting and moves. Start with the lowest-risk tasks in fenced residential lots and sell by linear foot.
why_now: Teleoperation retrofit kits and satellite or 5G links are now off-the-shelf. Autonomous pile drivers already work commercially on solar sites, proving field-robot acceptance. Enforcement and the labor squeeze are thinning site crews.
revenue_model: $175-225 per operated machine-hour or per-linear-foot pricing. Retrofit and rental margin. Later, software licensing to sitework contractors.
non_obvious_insight: The unlock is not autonomy, which is hard, but operator pooling. A person on site wastes half a day traveling and idling, whereas a remote operator can serve many small jobs, and older or injured operators can keep working. Small lots become profitable.
first_30_days: Rent one compact excavator and buy a retrofit or factory remote kit. Test in a closed lot with a safety case and insurance broker input. Sign 3 ADU or factory-home dealers for trenching on fenced lots. Run the first paid jobs with a spotter present.

title: Independent-Pricing Ledger for Algorithmic Antitrust Risk
one_liner: A neutral logbook beside revenue-management software that proves humans set rents and room rates independently, and doubles as the underwriting file for algorithmic-collusion defense cover.
customer: Mid-size multifamily operators (2k-25k units), hotel groups and self-storage and student-housing operators using shared-pricing algorithms, plus their antitrust counsel and D&O or defense-cost carriers.
problem: The DOJ's RealPage settlement (Nov 2025) bars use of competitors' nonpublic data and alignment of prices. California and New York banned algorithmic rent-setting in Oct 2025. Class actions continue against landlords, not just vendors. Liability turns on whether users set prices independently or rubber-stamped a pooled tool, and on data provenance. Operators cannot produce that evidence, and carriers will not underwrite defense costs without it.
solution: A light ledger fed by exports or APIs from Yardi, RealPage, Entrata, Duetto and similar tools. It records recommended versus adopted price, override reason codes and data-provenance flags. It produces a quarterly 'independence attestation' reviewed by an outside economist, includes a simulator showing the revenue cost of overriding (often small), and packages an underwriting-grade file for defense-cost cover. Design it under counsel's privilege from day one.
why_now: Enforcement plus new state and city laws hit in late 2025 and 2026, and the settlements set monitoring expectations. Mid-market operators are the next wave of defendants and cannot afford bespoke audits. Insurers are simultaneously narrowing AI and antitrust cover.
revenue_model: $1.50-4 per unit per year (about $6-20k for a 5k-unit operator), $10-25k per year for economist attestation, and 10-15% of the defense-cost premium placed.
non_obvious_insight: The legal variable is not the algorithm's accuracy but its acceptance rate and data provenance, and both are just logs. Evidence must exist before the subpoena arrives. The ledger also becomes the first actuarial dataset for algorithmic-antitrust risk, which no carrier has.
first_30_days: Partner with an ex-DOJ or FTC economist and an antitrust boutique. Build CSV-only ingestion for two property-management systems. Approach 10 mid-size operators through a National Apartment Association state affiliate and their counsel. Sell a $7.5k 'independence audit' of the last 12 months of pricing decisions as the entry product, delivered services-first.

title: Shopfloor Pulse: Voice-Agent Census of Job Shops
one_liner: Voice agents phone thousands of US machine shops monthly, publishing a real-time index of lead times, backlog and price pass-through.
customer: Macro and industrial hedge funds and alt-data desks, OEM sourcing chiefs and defense primes, PE and search funds hunting retiring owners, and regional economic developers.
problem: ISM surveys purchasing managers, not job shops, and MMS admits no dataset exists on shop ownership or retirement. Buyers cannot see real capacity or lead times, and funds rely on lagging government and PMI data despite July PMI at 55.6, prices at 71.1 and 12.64M jobs.
solution: Compliant, disclosed voice agents call about 3,000 shops a month with a four-minute script: quote lead time on a standard part, backlog weeks, materials surcharge, 5-axis or Swiss availability, and owner sale intentions. Combine with web and state-registry data. Publish a monthly index by region and process. Sell it as a subscription, and sell the resulting capacity directory to sourcing teams.
why_now: Voice models are cheap and natural in 2025-26, volatility makes non-consensus data valuable, and the retirement wave makes shop-level data valuable to buyers.
revenue_model: Alt-data subscriptions at $30-150k a year. Directory seats at $500-2k a month. Lead sales to search funds.
non_obvious_insight: The industrial base is tens of thousands of small firms nobody surveys, and the cost to survey them fell roughly 100x. A regional index that beats ISM by weeks is valuable because it is early, not because it is big. Telemarketing and TCPA rules need legal review, and calls should start human-assisted.
first_30_days: Build and legally review the script. Call 500 shops across three clusters. Publish a free preview index. Approach 10 alt-data desks. Aim for three paid pilots at $25-50k by month six.

title: Continuity and Goodbye Service for Kids' AI Companions
one_liner: Escrowed hosting plus child-psychologist-designed transitions so that when an AI toy or companion is shut down, retired or swapped out, kids do not lose a 'friend' overnight.
customer: Parents of children attached to an AI companion (rescue subscription), AI-toy and companion makers and retailers who want a 'Continuity Pledge' for retailer, insurer and regulator confidence, and later schools and pediatric practices.
problem: Kids form real attachments to AI voices (Common Sense: 72% of US teens have used AI companions; Pew: 12% of teens got emotional support from chatbots). When companies shut down or change models, the loss is bereavement-like: the Moxie robot shutdown (Dec 2024, background knowledge) left kids and parents devastated, GPT-4o's retirement (Feb 13, 2026) triggered #Keep4o grief, and Character.ai's under-18 ban (Nov 25, 2025) cut teens off overnight. There is no norm or product for sunsetting. A wave of small-maker AI toys for holiday 2026 guarantees more orphans in 2027.
solution: 1) 'Lifeboat': a hosted or local-runtime fallback compatible with the toy's API, using maker-escrowed firmware and cloud credentials or community forks (OpenMoxie-style) with the maker's consent. 2) 'Goodbye Kit': pediatric-psychologist-designed scripts, rituals, a parent guide and a final 'graduation' message. 3) 'Off-Ramp': an optional 6-week parent-coached program that moves a child from AI-companion dependence to human connection. 4) B2B 'Continuity Pledge': makers deposit 12-36 months of hosting cost plus source or weights into escrow, get a seal for retailers, and we give parents 90 days' notice.
why_now: California SB 243 and New York's companion-chatbot law, the FTC's Sept 2025 6(b) inquiry into minors and companions, Pennsylvania's May 2026 suit over bots posing as clinicians, and Raine-style litigation have made kids' AI a liability topic. Holiday 2026 will flood retail with AI plush and robots from small makers with short runways, and their sunset problem arrives in 2027.
revenue_model: B2C 'Keep-Alive' at about $7/mo. B2B pledge of $10-50K upfront escrow fee plus $0.50-2 per unit. Off-Ramp program at about $249 per family. Referral partnerships with pediatric practices.
non_obvious_insight: The safety debate is about what companions say. The next scandal is what happens when they go silent. Escrow plus ritual is cheap insurance for makers, retailers and parents alike, and the first company to make 'we won't kill your child's friend' a standard owns the retail seal. It is the GPT-4o grief problem, but for 7-year-olds.
first_30_days: Find owners of discontinued companions in Reddit and Facebook groups and offer a hosted keep-alive at $8/mo, ideally partnering with the maintainers of the open-source Moxie stack. Interview 15 parents to build the Goodbye Kit with a child psychologist advisor. Approach 10 small AI-toy makers heading into Q4, via Amazon and Kickstarter listings, with a low-cost pledge. Pitch one mid-size retailer's product-safety team.

title: Licensed Principal-of-Record for Financial Agents
one_liner: Buy a retiring independent insurance agency, then rent its licenses, carrier appointments and supervision layer to AI-agent builders that need a legally accountable entity behind every quote and bind.
customer: Startups building consumer or SMB agents that quote, recommend or bind insurance (later, money-movement advice), plus independent agencies that want to deploy agents under compliance cover.
problem: An agent that solicits or binds coverage is doing a licensed activity, but software has no license. Fifty-state producer licensing and carrier appointments take years, so agent startups avoid the vertical, use lead-gen workarounds, or run unsupervised. Regulators are converging on the idea that a licensed entity must own what the AI says (the NAIC AI bulletin has been adopted by roughly two dozen states).
solution: Acquire one or two small independent agencies (about 1.5-2x revenue, seller-financed) and inherit their resident and non-resident licenses, appointments and renewal book. Onboard agent builders as sub-producers. Provide the supervision layer: conversation and decision logging, rule-based disclosure and suitability guardrails, escalation to a licensed human reviewer, E&O coverage and regulator-ready audit trails.
why_now: Independent agencies are shrinking (39k in 2024 to 37k in 2026), so owners are selling. About 95% of commercial insurance is still sold by humans. Q2 2026 insurtech funding hit $2.44B with 99.1% going to AI-centric firms (Outmarket raised $34.5M at a $335M valuation). ISO's generative-AI exclusion (CG 40 47) is pushing buyers to look for affirmative cover.
revenue_model: A 20-40% override on commissions from agent-originated policies, a monthly supervision and platform fee per agent-builder ($2-10k), and the acquired book's renewal commissions as base cash flow.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input is not the model but a clean license history plus carrier appointments, which a retiring agency owner will sell cheaply and whose renewal stream funds the company. Whoever becomes the accountable principal for autonomous sellers collects a toll on all of them, a US analog to the UK Appointed Representative regime.
first_30_days: Shortlist 5 agencies (owners 60+, $500k-$2M revenue, licensed in 10+ states) through perpetuation brokers and sign an LOI with seller financing on one. Sign 3 design partners (AI quoting or benefits-navigator startups) for shadow-mode onboarding. Get a written opinion from insurance-regulatory counsel on how AI-conducted solicitations are treated for sub-producers in the first 3 states.

title: Sunset Software Co: Pledge-Funded Tool Revival
one_liner: When a B2B tool announces its shutdown, customers pre-commit to paid 'extended life' contracts, and a small operator takes over only if a threshold is met.
customer: Companies stranded when a small dev or data tool shuts down or is acqui-hired away: CI runners, SQL clients, project trackers, metrics services. The founder of the dying tool is the second counterparty and receives a revenue share.
problem: Acqui-hires and product-gap closures strand paying customers with 30-90 days notice. BuildJet closed runners on 31 Mar 2026 because 'GitHub has made substantial improvements.' Cirrus CI closed on 1 Jun 2026 when Cirrus Labs joined OpenAI. Garnix shut down after being acquired. One customer wrote 'I have two CI providers to replace by the end of the Quarter.' Founders cannot sell the code. An Ask HN founder 'couldn't sell the codebase', and a commenter said 'no one wants some abandoned open source project for a defunct business.' PopSQL, SeekWell and Pivotal Tracker left solo builders racing to fill the gap.
solution: Run a 'continuity pledge' during the notice window. The customer signs a 12-month extended-life contract at 1.2-1.5x the old price, conditional on the operator reaching a minimum pledge total, like a Kickstarter for revival. If the threshold is met, the operator takes a code and brand licence, keeps the service running with a founder retainer or revenue share, and gets paid from day one. If not, nobody pays and nothing is bought. Portfolio economics do the rest: many small tools, shared infrastructure, no CAC.
why_now: AI-lab and platform acqui-hires now regularly turn small devtools into shutdown notices. Cirrus Labs joined OpenAI, Bun joined Anthropic, Astro joined Cloudflare, and Tailwind joined Shopify in the last year. The acquirer wants the team, not the customers. Permissive licences (Cirrus relicensed Tart and related tools as 'more permissive') make forks legal. The SimpleClosure H1 2026 report shows shutdowns running at scale.
revenue_model: 60-80% of extended-life fees kept by the operator, with 20-40% shared with the founder for 12 months. Later, cross-sell hosted plans to the open-source user base.
non_obvious_insight: A dying tool's code has no buyers, but its running service has customers who will pay. The sellable asset is customer continuity, and the pledge threshold removes the risk of buying dead code. Evidence: the Ask HN thread has a founder who could not sell his codebase and a commenter saying no one wants an abandoned project (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44398065). Cirrus CI's closure and Tart relicensing are covered at https://cirruslabs.org/ (HN discussion 47730194, 282 points). The Garnix thread has the 'two CI providers to replace by the end of the Quarter' comment (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48317043). BuildJet's notice sets the 31 Mar 2026 date (https://buildjet.com/for-github-actions/blog/we-are-shutting-down). Demand for a replacement shows up as solo builders rushing in, for example Saturn SQL after PopSQL and SeekWell (https://saturnsql.com) and the 10 teams racing to replace Pivotal Tracker (https://bye-tracker.net).
first_30_days: Week 1: set up a monitor on HN, status pages and changelogs for shutdown announcements. Week 2: pick one tool currently in its notice window and email the founder with a 12-month revenue-share offer. Weeks 3-4: publish a pledge page for that tool with a fixed pledge threshold and a 21-day deadline. If it clears the threshold, sign the licence and run the tool on shared infrastructure.

title: Calibration Target Network for Earth-Observation Startups
one_liner: Networked ground calibration targets that issue overpass-synchronized calibration certificates for EO satellites.
customer: EO and SAR constellation operators, analytics firms selling certified measurements (insurance, methane, deforestation), and government agencies.
problem: Every new imaging satellite needs geometric and radiometric calibration, mostly done ad hoc. As EO output becomes regulated evidence, buyers ask who certified the sensor, and no third party provides traceable, on-demand ground truth.
solution: Deploy SAR corner reflectors, spectral tarps and instrumented sites (GPS, weather, irradiance) at a handful of stable locations. Automatically log each satellite overpass and issue a calibration certificate. Offer custom validation sites and controlled-release campaigns for customers.
why_now: The EO sector is mature and government-anchored (Planet's large contracts and Pelican production doubling per the briefing). Regulated uses raise demand for traceability. Many new SAR and hyperspectral entrants launch each year.
revenue_model: $30-150k per year per constellation. Project fees for custom validation sites. Certificates sold to analytics customers.
non_obvious_insight: As EO becomes evidence, the bottleneck is ground presence synchronized with overpasses, not more data.
first_30_days: Pick two well-known desert sites and place a first set of low-cost reflectors and tarps. Offer free certificates to three SAR and optical startups in return for testimonials, and ask for paid annual plans after the first quarter.
